activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
story:
The vending machine outside the cafeteria took Elijah's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like a small, personal insult, and he was still jiggling the coin return when Priya found him. She had her laptop under her arm the way she always did on Thursdays, the day she tallied orders for her sticker shop, and she was grinning.

"I cleared two hundred this month," she said. "After what I paid for the printer ink and the mailing envelopes and the paper. Two hundred dollars of actual profit."

Elijah gave up on the machine and followed her to the bench by the trophy case, where she opened the laptop on her knees. The spreadsheet was neat, almost fussy; every expense had a receipt number beside it. She scrolled through it slowly, savoring it, and he could see that the numbers did what she said. Money in, money out, and a tidy remainder in green.

"How many hours?" he asked.

She stopped scrolling. "What?"

"How many hours did it take? Designing, printing, cutting, packing, walking to the post office."

She looked at the screen differently then, the way you look at a staircase you've climbed without counting the steps. "I don't know. Maybe... three a night? Four on weekends. Call it eighty since September."

He did it in his head, not to be cruel but because he couldn't not. Eighty hours, even at the babysitting rate, the tutoring rate, the rate for scooping ice cream at the stand by the highway where they'd both applied last spring. She wasn't ahead. She was somewhere behind, and the green number was still glowing at the bottom of her screen like a firefly that had wandered into a jar.

"So it's not real," Priya said. It wasn't quite a question.

"It's real," Elijah said. "It's just not the whole real. What you subtracted, everything you actually paid money for, that part's called accounting profit. But if you also subtract what your own hours would've earned somewhere else, that's economic profit. That's the one that knows about you."

She shut the laptop halfway, then opened it again, as if the numbers might have rearranged themselves out of pity. Down the hall, Mr. Okafor was trying to make the drama kids pick up their backpacks before rehearsal, and everyone was ignoring him, and he kept saying "I will not be a despot about this" until the word lost its shape. Priya watched the hallway instead of her spreadsheet.

"My dad said the shop would teach me business," she said. "It did. Just not the lesson he ordered."

They sat with that. Elijah thought about his own ledger, the one nobody printed for you: the summer job he'd turned down to take a drawing class, the class he'd taken instead of driving lessons, the way every yes seemed to quietly underwrite a no he never got to read. He had been half-dozing through it for years, calling it scheduling. Priya's spreadsheet had just put columns on it.

"Okay," she said finally, and her voice had the flat calm of someone deciding something. "I could raise prices. Or I could quit and tutor, and make more, and be bored." She looked at him. "Which one's the smart one?"

He wanted to tell her that the smart one existed, that somewhere in every choice there was a version with no remainder, but the honest answer was that he didn't know, and he found he'd rather say that than hand her a doctrine. "I don't think there's a smart one," he said. "There's just the one you'd rather regret less."

"That's a terrible thing to tell someone."

"I know."

She laughed, closed the laptop all the way, and stood. Then she walked back toward the vending machine, fed it a dollar of her supposed profit, and pressed the button for the peanut bar. The coil turned. The bar tipped forward, hung at the lip of the shelf, and stopped, half in and half out, refusing both the floor and her hand.

"See," Elijah said, "even the candy knows."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
Nathaniel had claimed the corner table at Coraggio's with a latte, a library copy of a style manual, and the growing suspicion that his history teacher had invented footnotes as a form of torture. The assignment was due in nine days: an argument, not a report, with evidence and a bibliography in proper form. He had chosen to argue that the New Deal's rural electrification programs mattered less for the electricity than for the infrastructure of expertise they left behind, which sounded impressive until he tried to write the second sentence.

Priya slid into the opposite chair, uninvited, carrying a smoothie the color of pond water. "I've been at this paper since seven a.m.," she announced, "and I have achieved a breakthrough. I found this historian who says exactly what I want to say about the Marshall Plan, and I put the whole paragraph into my own words. Every single word. So now it's mine." She said this the way other people announced lottery wins.

"Wait," Nathaniel said. "You didn't cite it?"

"Why would I? I didn't copy anything. There's not one sentence that matches." She flipped her laptop around to show him, radiating the smugness of someone who believed she had discovered a loophole in the academic legal code. Priya's actual goal, he had gradually understood, was not to write a great paper but to finish by Thursday, two days early, so she could claim the weekend for a trip to the coast her parents kept threatening to cancel. Speed was her religion.

Nathaniel, who had spent forty minutes that morning being lectured by the style manual, felt the malaise of a man who knows just enough to ruin everyone's afternoon. He dragged the manual across the table, licked his thumb, and found the page. "Listen to this part." He read aloud the sentence about how putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.

Priya stared at him. "That's absurd. I changed the words."

"You changed the words. The idea's still hers." He tapped the page. "You're borrowing her thinking without her name on it."

"You are about to pontificate," Priya said, pointing her smoothie straw at him like a weapon. "I can feel it coming. Don't."

"I'm not pontificating, I'm quoting. There's a difference. Pontificating is what Mr. Halvard does about comma splices." He was pleased with this, and she cracked a smile despite herself, which he took as a small victory in their long-running war of who got to be insufferable that day.

She slumped, chin on her fist. "So I have to go back through everything and figure out which ideas are mine and which ones I absorbed from reading at midnight. Half of them I don't even remember where they came from." This, Nathaniel thought, was the genuinely unsettling part, and he did not say so, because she had told him not to pontificate and he was trying to be a person who listened. Somewhere between her third and fourth paragraph he had realized the same trap was waiting in his own draft: he had reworded a line about the Tennessee Valley Authority so smoothly that he had half convinced himself he'd thought of it on the bus.

"You could do what the manual says," he offered instead. "Cite the ones you remember, and flag the ones you don't, and check them against your sources. I'll trade you. You read my argument and tell me if it actually says anything, and I'll help you hunt down your ghost ideas." The deal was transparently in her favor, and they both knew it, and Priya accepted anyway, because the coast was two days away and time had made her ductile on the subject of pride.

They worked until the café's afternoon light went long and gold across the table, Priya reading his thesis aloud in a terrible British accent while he winced, then both of them flipping through her sources, finding the historian's fingerprint on sentence after sentence she had sworn was original. The barista came by with a rag and asked, without any real curiosity, whether they were studying. "Torture," Priya said. "Court-sanctioned."

Nathaniel looked at his own draft, at the paragraph he now knew he owed a footnote to, and did not write the footnote yet. He underlined it instead, twice, the way you mark a door you intend to come back through.

"That one?" Priya asked, watching him.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
story:
Peyton pushed through the library doors with her poster board rolled under one arm like a club, and went straight to the periodicals room in the back, where the microfiche machine hummed under a fluorescent light nobody had ever bothered to fix. Her science fair project had won second place. Second, not first, because three classmates on the judging panel had asked her to repeat her bacteria-count in front of them and the numbers came out different the second time, and she had stood there feeling her face go hot while they exchanged looks.

She had not come to hide. She had come to prove them wrong, or to prove something, though she was not yet sure what. The librarian on duty, a small woman named Mrs. Okafor who kept a jar of peppermints for the after-school crowd, watched Peyton wrestling with the microfiche drawer and came over without being asked. "You look like someone hunting a specific fact," Mrs. Okafor said, "and the drawer is winning."

"Something about how scientists are supposed to act," Peyton said. "There has to be a rule. One experiment can't just be thrown out because somebody asks a question about it." She had spent the bus ride composing arguments in her head, transcribing the angriest of them into her notebook so she could deliver them with precision later.

Mrs. Okafor tilted her head. "Sociology shelf, maybe. The scientists have studied themselves, you know. Somebody had to." She pointed toward the stacks and went back to the desk, and Peyton followed the pointing finger past a table where a boy from her civics class was spreading out photocopies about prison reform, muttering the word recidivism to himself as he highlighted. She almost stopped to ask him whether a person could be right and doubted at the same time, but she kept walking.

The book was older than her mother, a dusty sociology reader with a cracked spine, and she found the page by accident, flipping past chapters on everything else. In 1942, a sociologist named Robert K. Merton had written about the norms of science, and one of them was called organized skepticism. She read the phrase twice. Claims had to survive critical scrutiny by the community before they were accepted. Not one claim, one judge, one afternoon. The community. She sat down on the floor between the shelves with the book open on her knees and felt something rearrange itself in her chest, and it was not entirely pleasant.

Because it cut both ways. If the classmates who questioned her result were doing what scientists were supposed to do, then her result, the one she had counted on, was not yet knowledge at all. It was a claim. It had not survived anything yet. And if she wanted it to be real, the way to get there was not a sharper argument on the bus, it was doing the count again, and again after that, and writing down every failure as carefully as every success.

She checked the book out, using the last dollar of her penurious allowance to pay off an old late fee so Mrs. Okafor could stamp the card, and carried it back to the periodicals room. The boy with the prison articles was still there, stabbing at his highlighter. "You ever cite something and have people just not believe it?" she asked him.

"All the time," he said. "That's kind of the point, though, isn't it? If it holds up anyway, it counts for more." He slid one of his peppermints, which he must have gotten from the desk, across the table to her without comment, and she took it.

On Monday she got to the biology lab before first period and set up the Petri dishes again, and when her friend Dana leaned in the doorway and said, "I thought you were done with that," Peyton said, "Apparently it's not done with me." She wrote the date at the top of a fresh data sheet, counted the first plate twice, and started the tally.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
The satellite dish at the Okafor house had died two days before the final, so everyone crowded into Zoe's neighbor Mr. Delgado's living room instead, eighteen people in a room built for six, folding chairs in the aisles like a tiny stadium. Zoe ended up on the arm of the couch between her father and her cousin Marcus, who had spent the whole tournament explaining the game to her as though she hadn't watched it with Grandpa since she was nine. It was July 2018 and the whole month had felt like this, everyone declaring themselves an authority, the television commentators lionize this striker or that midfielder while the actual play went on underneath all the talk.

What Zoe wanted, and had wanted since the group stage, was for Marcus to be wrong once, publicly, in front of the family that treated him as the resident genius. He had gotten away with a month of confident nonsense. In the round of sixteen he had sworn that France's winner against Argentina was offside when it wasn't. When the goal stood, he'd said the linesman missed it, and nobody challenged him because nobody else knew. Zoe knew. Grandpa had taught her the offside law with saltshakers on a kitchen table, walking the pepper grinder slowly forward until the moment of the pass. That was the summer before he died, and she had kept watching partly to keep something of his going.

In the eighty-seventh minute, with the score tied, a forward went down in the box under a defender's trailing leg. The referee pointed to the penalty spot immediately, and half the room roared while the other half groaned. Marcus stood up with his arms out. "That's a dive," he announced. "And it doesn't matter anyway, they can't take back a penalty once he's given it. Refs can't review anything, that's the whole point, the call on the field stands."

Zoe felt her heart kick, because this was it, this was the moment she'd been waiting a month for, and she also felt something uglier underneath, the smallness of wanting it so badly. "They can review it," she said. Her voice came out quieter than she'd planned, and several heads turned. "This is the first World Cup with video assistant referees. Russia, this year. They've been checking goals and penalties all tournament." She could hear Grandpa's phrasing in her own mouth, the way he'd said penalties with a little lift at the end, pleased with the word.

"It's called VAR," said Mr. Delgado's daughter Priya, without looking up from her phone, and on the screen the referee had already stopped play and touched his finger to his ear, circling his other hand in the air. Zoe watched the box on the broadcast freeze the image, draw its lines, hold everyone in the room suspended between hope and grievance. "They can review goals, penalties, red cards," she went on, steadier now. "Even if a ref gives a card to the wrong player, the wrong guy entirely, they can fix it. That actually happened somewhere, Grandpa told me. Mistaken identity."

"Your grandpa told you a lot of things," Marcus said, but he said it toward the television, not at her, and Zoe understood it as the closest thing to a retreat he knew how to make. The wait stretched on. Her father, who had spent weeks deferring to Marcus on every contested call, kept glancing at Zoe with an expression she couldn't read, and she thought about all the times she'd stayed quiet at that same table, how easy the silence had been, what it had cost nothing to keep. She wondered whether speaking up now was brave or just late.

The referee jogged back toward the spot, raised the whistle to his lips, and awarded the penalty. The room detonated. Marcus threw his hands up in vindication, already rewriting history aloud: he'd never doubted the review system, he'd only questioned this particular decision, which was, frankly, incisive of him. Zoe's team was still losing, though. The penalty was converted in the ninetieth minute, and the comeback she'd wanted all match died with it, and she sat on the arm of the couch watching a room full of Delgados celebrate a result she had spent ninety minutes rooting against.

Afterward, while the adults argued about the referee's fitness, Priya slid her phone across the cushion toward Marcus. "You said refs can't review anything," she said. "You said that, out loud, two minutes before they reviewed the thing." Marcus read the screen, which confirmed every word Zoe had said, and something in his face closed like a door. Zoe waited for the pleasure she'd been owed. It came, a brief hot flash of it, watching him trapped in front of everyone by her grandfather's facts, delivered in her grandfather's cadence.

Then it drained away and left her with the strange arithmetic of the evening: she had been right, she had finally said so, and the only result was that her team had lost, her cousin had lost, and the reprieve of silence she'd enjoyed all tournament was gone for good. There would be no more sitting quietly in the corner with a private certainty. Her father put his hand briefly on her shoulder on the way to the kitchen and said, "Saltshakers," and nothing else. Zoe looked at the frozen replay still looping on the screen, the forward suspended mid-fall, neither diving nor fouled, forever unresolvable, and heard Marcus behind her say, "Next World Cup, I'm sitting next to you."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
story:
Room 214 smelled of dry-erase marker and the radiator's scorched dust, and the math club had pushed its desks into the crooked horseshoe it always pushed them into, as though geometry could be improvised. Kyle sat with his pencil already moving, because the regional problem set was due Friday and he was three problems behind Priya, who kept score even when nobody asked her to.

Ms. Okafor had left a warm-up on the board: find the derivative of a polynomial and use it to locate the maximum. Below it she'd written two functions, f of x equals three x squared minus twelve x and g of x equals three x squared minus twelve x plus seven, and the instruction to differentiate both. She was out in the hall arguing with the copier, which meant the room belonged to whoever spoke loudest.

Priya finished in ninety seconds, flat-handed her paper, and read her answers aloud. "Both of them have derivative six x minus twelve. Maximum at x equals two."

"That's wrong," said Deshawn, without looking up. He had a sardonic way of saying things were wrong, chin dipped, like the error had personally inconvenienced him. "They can't both be the same. They're different functions. I got six x minus twelve for f, but for g I got six x minus twelve plus seven. Somebody copied the problem wrong."

Kyle had gotten the same thing as Priya, and for a moment the old reflex rose in him, the one that said two answers to one problem means one of them is garbage and it's probably his. He'd spent two years treating math as a slot where a single correct coin had to drop, and every time his coin bounced out he retreated. But last month his older sister had told him that in her lab, two people getting different results was the beginning of the interesting part, not the end, and he'd been turning that over since, unsure whether it applied to a Tuesday afternoon in a borrowed classroom.

He pulled his paper closer. He checked the g function term by term, tracing each digit with his pencil tip to keep his eyes honest. Three x squared. Minus twelve x. Plus seven. He hadn't copied it wrong, and neither had Priya, because her sheet matched his, and he could see Deshawn's sheet from here and the seven was there too, sitting at the end like a period.

"Wait," Kyle said. "Where did you get the extra seven in your derivative?"

"From the seven in the function," Deshawn said, in the tone of a man explaining doors to someone who had walked through several.

Kyle didn't answer right away. He wrote the seven by itself on the edge of his paper, then wrote zero under it, then crossed out the zero, because he wasn't sure yet and he didn't want to perform a confidence he didn't have. What he remembered from Monday's notes was a single line, almost a throwaway: the derivative of a constant is zero. If that was true, then the seven in g contributed nothing to the derivative, nothing at all, and six x minus twelve would be the answer for both, exactly what Priya had said, and exactly what he'd gotten before doubt made him want to hide his paper.

He tried it the other way first, because that was only fair. If Deshawn were right, the derivatives would differ by seven, and the maxima would land in different places, which would mean two functions that were plainly related, one just shifted upward, would peak at different x values. Kyle sketched both graphs quickly, freehand, the same curve drawn twice, the second one lifted bodily above the first. The peaks sat on the same vertical line. He drew the line and tapped it twice with his pencil.

"Deshawn," he said. "Adding seven to a function shifts its graph up but leaves its derivative unchanged. So the derivative's the same for both. Same maximum, x equals two." He said it and then, because he was trying to be the kind of person who admitted the seams, added, "I'm sure about the graph. I'm less sure why the constant dies in the rule, only that it does."

Deshawn came around the horseshoe and bent over Kyle's sketch, close enough that Kyle could smell the gum he was forever chewing. He looked for a long time. Somewhere near the window, Marcus was telling a story about his biology teacher's obsession with speciation, how one population splits into two and both go on as if the split never happened, and Kyle thought, not for the first time, that math and biology were always eavesdropping on each other. Then Deshawn straightened up.

"The graphs," he said. His voice had lost its armor. "The graphs are the same shape." He sat down, pulled his paper back, and drew a hard line through the plus seven in his derivative. He didn't say Kyle was right. He started rechecking everything from the beginning, which was its own kind of concession, and Priya, watching him do it, permitted herself one small exhale that might have been a laugh.

Kyle looked at his own page, at the same answer written twice for two different functions, and felt something he could only call the ordinary kind of exhilarated, the small clean lift of a door coming unlocked. He still didn't understand why the constant vanished; he understood that it did, and that a shifted curve kept its shape, and that two people could square up over an answer and both walk away holding pieces of the truth. Ms. Okafor came back in with a stack of photocopies and a look of grim victory, and began dealing them down the horseshoe like cards.

Kyle took his copy and wrote his name at the top, then, underneath, in small letters, the two functions side by side with an arrow between them, up seven, same derivative, a note to a future self who would probably need it.

"Same time Thursday?" Priya asked, gathering her things before the second bell.

"Same time," Kyle said, and zipped his pencil case shut over the sound of the radiator ticking.

story:
Jordan had been the last cut his junior year, so when Coach Priddy kept him this season, he decided he would earn the roster spot by becoming the one player who never took a bad shot. He studied his own percentages in a notebook he kept in his backpack, and by the third week of practice he had a habit that the other guys noticed: if he missed two in a row, he passed the next three times, no matter how open he was.

"You're doing it wrong," Dev said one Tuesday in the gym off Fairmount Avenue, sitting on the scorer's table with his laptop balanced on his knees. Dev was the backup point guard and the only person Jordan knew who read economics papers for fun. "You think streaks aren't real, so you punish yourself for missing. That's backwards."

The practice had thinned out to six guys shooting around. Jordan wiped sweat off his forehead with the hem of his shirt and came over. "The research says the hot hand is a myth. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody knows the old study. The famous one, from 1985. But in 2018 two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, showed that analysis had a statistical bias, and they found evidence of streak shooting in the same data." Dev turned the laptop so Jordan could see the paper, dense with symbols Jordan didn't follow, but he caught the names and the years. "The same data," Dev said again, tapping the screen. "The stuff that was supposed to prove there's no such thing actually proved there is, once you fix the math."

Jordan wanted to dismiss it, because dismissing things was easier than admitting he had organized his whole season around a mistake. But Dev was the kind of person who was never blase about being right; he printed out pages and carried them around folded into his shoes. That part Jordan had to respect.

The next game was away, a gym that smelled like popcorn and floor wax, the bleachers close enough that Jordan could hear individual conversations when the clock stopped. He started the first half two for nine, all jumpers, all taken because the shot clock was dying rather than because he wanted them. In the third quarter he hit one from the elbow, clean, and then another off a curl, and he felt something loosen in his shoulders that had been tight since November.

Here was the problem, and Jordan stood at the free throw line during a timeout and tried to look at it honestly instead of picking the version that flattered him. If he trusted the streak now, was that judgment or was it excuse? The old Jordan, the notebook Jordan, would have said you never lift your head above the numbers, that discipline calcifies into something you can stand on. But Dev's paper was numbers too. Two rigorous ways of thinking, and they pointed in opposite directions, and there was no referee standing at midcourt to say which one owned him tonight.

He got the ball on the right wing with forty seconds left and his team down two. The defender sagged off him, the whole gym apparently agreeing with the 1985 version of Jordan, the one who would swing the ball and let someone else decide. Dev was calling for it at the top, open, and for a full breath Jordan held both possibilities, the pass and the shot, the caution and the streak, neither one fully provable.

He shot.

The ball hit the back rim, climbed, and dropped through, and the net made its small dry sound while the crowd was still inhaling. Dev ran at him with both hands raised, shouting something Jordan couldn't separate from the noise. On the walk back up the floor, the other team's coach was red-faced at his clipboard, and Jordan thought, not for the first time, that the truth probably wasn't one thing or the other, and that he'd take the uncertainty if it came with nights like this.

"Same data," Dev said, grinning, as they set the defense. "Same data."

story:
Ryan had promised his grandmother he would practice while she was in the hospital, which was how he came to be alone in her living room with the upright piano, a beginner's book, and no idea what he was doing. The book's first page showed a keyboard diagram with letters on it, and Ryan, who trusted nothing he hadn't counted himself, decided to count the keys before he played a single note. He started with the white ones, touching each lightly so the hammers wouldn't sound, and lost his place twice when the phone rang, but he got there in the end: fifty-two. The black keys came next, thirty-six of them, and when he added the two together he got eighty-eight, which felt less like arithmetic and more like discovering the piano had been keeping a secret from him. Eighty-eight doors, and he could open none of them.

His grandmother had left the book open to "Hot Cross Buns," a song he had assumed was beneath him until he tried it. His fingers landed like dropped potatoes. He played E, E, E and the note came out wrong somehow, and when he hunted for the reason he found it in his own hand: he'd been aiming for a black key, thinking it was white, because in the middle of the keyboard the pattern blurred. He laughed at himself, alone in the room, which felt ridiculous and also fine.

When his cousin Devi arrived to water the plants, she found him hunched over the middle of the keyboard like a man trying to defuse it. "You look destitute," she said, dropping her backpack. "Like a pianist who lost everything in the war."

"I lost the note E," Ryan said. "It moved."

"Keys don't move. That's the whole appeal of pianos." She came and stood beside him, and he noticed she wasn't laughing at him exactly, more near him, the way people laugh during a storm. He showed her the problem: the black keys came in twos and threes, and he kept miscounting which group he was in, so his hand drifted like a car into the wrong lane. Devi, who played flute and therefore considered herself above keyboard problems, began to pontificate about how piano was obviously the easy instrument because everything was laid out in front of you, nothing to tune, nothing to guess. Ryan listened, then pointed at the keyboard.

"Then find me E," he said.

She found it instantly, and he hated her for two full seconds, and then he saw how she'd done it. The black keys weren't decoration; they were signposts. Find a group of two, and E sat immediately to the right of it, every time, all the way up. The pattern that had been a morass of identical ivories a minute ago snapped into landmarks, like a street where suddenly all the houses have numbers.

They spent the next hour in a contest Devi invented on the spot, which was to name a letter and slap the correct key before the other person could. Ryan lost eleven times in a row, then began to win, then began to win on purpose, calling out the letters in a singsong to throw her off. She retaliated by calling out letters in alphabetical order, which was harder than it sounded, because the piano's alphabet ran out at G and started over, wrapping around like a wheel. "Who designed this," Devi demanded, missing an A. "Who said seven letters and then we start over, like it's a roller coaster."

"Some dead German, probably," Ryan said, and played his "Hot Cross Buns," all the way through, with every note where it belonged. It was a small, dumb song and he played it like it was a national anthem. Then, because it felt like cheating not to, he tried it an octave higher, and it worked, and he tried it again starting on a different note entirely, and it didn't sound like "Hot Cross Buns" anymore but it didn't sound wrong either, exactly, just like the same tune wearing someone else's coat. He didn't know what to make of that, and said so.

"That's the piano doing piano things," Devi said. "Not your problem yet."

But it sat in his head anyway, that shifting, as he practiced the song once more, clean and slow, fifty-two white keys under his hands and thirty-six black ones waiting like the second half of a language he hadn't learned. He had started the afternoon thinking the keyboard was a wall. Now it seemed more like a map, though of what, he genuinely couldn't say. He found his grandmother's phone number where she'd left it by the lamp, next to the hospital's, and dialed, drumming two black keys with his free hand while it rang.

"Grandma," he said when she picked up. "It's eighty-eight keys. I counted."

story:
The book club met on Tuesdays at his grandmother's house, and Brayden had been attending all summer because his mother thought it would keep him from his phone. It had worked, in a way. He had read The Great Gatsby in four sittings on the porch swing, and now, standing in the kitchen with iced tea sweating against his palm, he was trying to decide whether he actually liked the narrator. Nick Carraway seemed like a decent guy, the kind who held back judgment the way you'd hold back a dog on a leash. That was the sentence Brayden kept returning to, the one he'd underlined twice: "I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known." It had the ring of a man introducing himself at a party, hand out, shoulders square.

"I think the whole book turns on that line," he said when Mrs. Okafor, who taught retired schoolteachers how to knit, asked what he'd thought of the ending. "He tells you he's honest, so you believe everything after that."

Mrs. Okafor set down her needles. "Does he, though," she said, and it wasn't a question so much as a door swinging open.

His grandmother carried in a plate of lemon squares and the club settled around the good room, the one with plastic on nothing anymore but the couch still smelled faintly of lavender. Mrs. Okafor started listing things, counting them off on her fingers like items on a grocery receipt. Nick never tells Daisy that Tom has a mistress, or at least not when it might matter. Nick claims to reserve judgment in the third chapter and then judges nearly everyone in the book. Nick says he's honest in a novel published in 1925, and then, in that same novel, he helps Gatsby arrange a meeting with Daisy behind Tom's back and never says a word to anyone about the woman Myrtle's husband is looking for at the end.

Brayden felt the porch swing, the four sittings, the underlining, all of it begin to tilt. "But he tells us those things," he said. "He confesses. He admits he disliked Gatsby at first."

"He confesses the small things," said Mr. Delgado from the armchair, "so we'll trust him with the large ones."

That night Brayden lay in the foldout bed in his grandmother's sewing room, the mattress bar suturing itself into his spine no matter how he arranged the quilts, and he wondered whether a narrator could be lying and telling the truth at once. He thought about how his little cousin told you she hadn't eaten a cookie with chocolate still on her mouth, and how you believed her anyway because she was so open about everything else. Was Nick like that? Or was the cookie evidence the whole point?

He got up and found his copy on the dresser, and by lamplight he reread the first pages, the ones where Nick reports what his father told him and then quietly folds it into his own opinion, so smoothly you couldn't see the seam. In the morning, over eggs, his grandmother asked what he was scribbling in the margins, and he showed her a page where he'd written "borrowed authority" and then, lower down, "but whose eyes?" He said he had started the summer thinking the book was about Gatsby, and now he thought it was about whether you could trust the person telling you about Gatsby, which was a different book hiding inside the first one, the way the reflection of the sound sat under the water.

"That's rather the point of an unreliable narrator," Mrs. Okafor said at the next meeting, when he laid it all out, the two columns he'd made, moments where Nick bent things and moments where he didn't. "The author builds the crack into the wall on purpose. Being suspicious of everything is a disincentive to enjoying fiction, of course. You can't read if you trust no one." She took a lemon square. "The trick is deciding how much to withhold."

Brayden said he still wasn't sure. Nick seemed honest about his dishonesty, which felt like a paradox, except it also felt exactly like everyone he knew at school, including himself. He had an inchoate sense that the answer wasn't yes or no but something shaped like a bell curve, most of Nick trustworthy, the edges of him not, and he hadn't yet figured out which parts were edges.

"So what do you think?" his grandmother asked him on the porch that evening, the swing chains creaking under their combined weight, the sound gone pewter-colored in the dusk. "Is he honest?"

Brayden looked out at the yard, where the fireflies were starting up along the fence line, and turned the question over one more time. "He's honest the way a photograph is honest," he said. "Everything in the frame is true. But he's the one holding the camera."

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The restaurant smelled of rosemary and burnt butter, and Loic told himself he belonged there, which was the first thing he got wrong that afternoon, though not the last. He was eighteen, the interview had gone well, and the manager, a compact woman named Dara, had said the word "hired" before he had even sat down. That was how easy it was, he decided. He had always been good at seeming like the kind of person people wanted.

She handed him a clipboard in the back office, between racks of canned tomatoes and a wall calendar with someone's shift penciled in. "Fill this out while I check the walk-in," she said, and left him alone with a pen chained to the clipboard.

The first page asked for his name, his address, his Social Security number, all of which he knew. The second page did not. It wanted allowances and withholdings and a word he could not pronounce in his head, and the form was called a Form W-4, which meant nothing to him. He could have asked Dara. Instead he texted his mother, because asking Dara would have meant admitting he did not already know, and Loic had built this whole afternoon on the principle that he already knew things.

His mother was at work and slow to answer. While he waited, he inventoried the office: a cosmopolitan collection of hot sauces from three continents lined the shelf above the desk, as if the kitchen's ambitions had overflowed into the paperwork. He liked that. It made the place feel bigger than a strip-mall bistro, and he wanted, more than he had admitted to anyone, for his life to feel bigger than it was.

His phone buzzed. "It's the form so your employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck," his mother wrote. "Don't guess at the boxes. Read them."

He read them. He read them again. Somewhere in the middle of the second reading, he understood that he had been narrating this day to himself all wrong. He had been telling himself the story of a boy casually picking up a summer job, a boy with options, who could take it or leave it. The truth, which he had been stepping around like a wet spot on the kitchen floor, was that his father had been out of work since March, and the household bank account was not a topic at dinner anymore, it was a silence with plates around it. Nobody had asked Loic to work. Nobody had said he couldn't. He had simply decided, in the wordless way families decide things, that he would.

That was the fact he had been withholding from himself, and now it sat there on the clipboard, patient as a tax form.

He tried to contextualize it, the way his sociology teacher would have wanted: an eighteen-year-old in a rich country, taking a first job in a restaurant, one small data point in a vast economy. But causality was harder to dress up than that. His father's layoff had happened; therefore Loic was here; therefore he was squinting at boxes about dependents and other income. The chain felt less like sociology and more like dominoes.

Dara came back wiping her hands on a towel. "Stuck?"

"The boxes," he said. "On the W-4." He heard the sentence he almost said instead, the breezy one, the one that would have claimed he'd done this before at his uncle's shop, which did not exist. He let it die. "I've never done taxes. I don't want to put the wrong thing and mess up my paychecks."

"Smart not to guess," Dara said. She pulled a chair around and set it beside him, not across, which he noticed. "Read each line, answer what's true for you, and if two answers seem true, there's a worksheet for that."

He worked through it slowly, and she waited without hovering, checking the calendar, saying nothing. When he finished, he signed his name in the last open box, and the signature looked different from the one on his learner's permit, older, or maybe just smaller.

"You start Saturday, four o'clock," Dara said, taking the clipboard. "Black pants, nonslip shoes. And Loic, whatever's on that form, it's just the government's part. The rest of the job is showing up."

He walked out through the dining room, past a family of five splitting three entrees, and stood in the parking lot where the afternoon heat came up off the asphalt. He texted his mother back. "Done. Saturday I start." Then, before he could edit himself into someone breezier, he typed, "Tell Dad it's handled," and pressed send.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Landon had counted on the drive up to finish his geography packet, but the road had turned to washboard gravel two miles back, and every bump sent the pencil skidding across the population pyramid he was trying to copy. His grandfather drove with both wrists over the wheel, unhurried, as though the mountain were not going anywhere. It was not. The packet was due Monday, and Monday was forty hours away, and there was no signal at the campsite, which Landon had known and had chosen to ignore.

"I printed everything," his grandfather said at the trailhead, hoisting a canvas duffel that had to be older than Landon's mother. "The whole set of charts. My phone does that now, but I don't trust it in the trees." He said this without apology, the way he said most things, and Landon, who trusted nothing without bars in the corner, carried the duffel up the switchbacks in silence.

The packet asked a question Landon could not get past: given a country's population pyramid, decide whether that country would need more schools or more nursing homes in twenty years, and defend the answer. He had assumed the answer would be obvious, the way answers had been obvious all through high school, and the fact that it was not obvious felt like a personal defect. By the time the tent was up and the stove was hissing, he had the charts spread across the picnic table, weighted with flat stones against the wind.

"Those are pyramids," his grandfather said, looking over his shoulder while slicing an onion on a cutting board balanced on a stump. "They call them population pyramids. They didn't look like pyramids much even when I learned them, and that was in an antiquated classroom with a chalkboard and a teacher who smelled of pipe smoke." He went back to the onion. That was all he offered, which Landon would later understand as a kind of mercy.

The chart for their own country was the one that stopped him. He had expected a pyramid, a shape wide at the bottom and narrowing toward the top, the way the textbook's example of a young country looked. Instead the middle of the shape bulged, and the base beneath it was narrower. He kept turning the paper, as if the angle were the problem. The bars for the youngest groups were shorter than the bars for people his parents' age. Somewhere in the back of his mind a sentence from the packet assembled itself: a pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population. He traced the middle bars with one finger, then the base, then back, and felt the two facts slide against each other like plates.

"So in twenty years," he said aloud, mostly to the stove, "all these people in the middle are old. And there aren't as many coming up behind them." He looked at the youngest bars again, the narrow base. Fewer children now meant fewer adults later, and the wide middle meant many adults aging at once. "Nobody's building schools for that. They're going to need nursing homes. Elder care. A lot of it." His grandfather only nodded at the onions, letting him own the sentence, and Landon sat with the small strange vertigo of seeing his own country as a shape on paper, as a thing with a future that could be read.

The trouble came at the second chart, a genuinely young country, wide at the base, and Landon wrote "schools" quickly and then stopped. It was not that simple, and he knew it, and the knowing irritated him. He wanted a rule he could apply cleanly, the way he applied formulas in calculus, and the charts were refusing to be formulas. He thought of his mother, who worked nights at a care facility three towns over, who came home with her scrubbs smelling of disinfectant and her shoulders inure to a weight Landon had never once seen her set down. Who staffed the homes in a country whose base was narrowing? He wrote the question in the margin of the packet, then crossed it out, then wrote it again, smaller.

Deadline pressure arrived with the light. His flashlight had a third of its charge, the stove fuel was measured for two mornings, and the packet had to be complete before they hiked out Sunday noon, because Monday morning was the presentation and there would be no time after. So he worked while his grandfather washed the dishes in the dark basin, working through country after country, testing his reading against the shapes. The substrate of his notebook page grew soft where his palm rested, and he moved his hand, and kept going.

At some point his grandfather sat down across the table with two cups of tea and said nothing, which was his way of sitting with somebody. Landon held up the chart of their own country in the flashlight beam, the narrow base, the swelling middle, and said, "This one's us. In twenty years." His grandfather looked at it a long moment, then at his grandson, then out toward the black line of the trees.

"Better figure out who's going to pour the coffee in those homes," he said, and drank.

story:
The trumpet had belonged to James's grandfather, and it arrived on Tuesday in a box that smelled of attic and machine oil, packed in newspaper so old the headlines had gone diaphanous, the print ghosting through onto the bell of the horn. The audition was Saturday. Four days. James had told Ms. Ferro, the community band director, that he could play, which was a lie built from a half-truth: he could read music, four years of school clarinet, but he had never touched a trumpet in his life.

"You said Saturday," his father said from the kitchen doorway, arms folded. "That's not four days of learning an instrument. That's four days of noise."

"Then it's four days of noise," James said, and put the mouthpiece to his lips.

The first sounds were worse than noise. They were something the horn seemed to extrude from deep in its tubing, flat and blatting, a diseased duck. His father left the room. James kept going, because the alternative was admitting to Ms. Ferro that he'd lied, and he'd already told his cousin Deej he was in, and Deej had told three other people.

On Wednesday he found the tuner. It was at the bottom of the box, a little clip-on device with a screen, still holding a charge after who knew how many years. He clipped it to the bell, played what he believed was an A, and watched the needle swing and settle. The screen read 440. He frowned at that, played again, held it steady. 440. The A was in tune, apparently, whatever tune meant, and the machine agreed with him.

Then he tried the A an octave up, the way the fingering chart in his method book showed it, and the screen jumped. Not to 445, not to 450. To 880. He sat very still on the edge of his bed with the horn warm in his hands. He played the low A. 440. The high A. 880. Exactly double, both times, and a third time, and a fourth, the digits landing clean with no wobble in between.

"Deej," he said into his phone, "what's A440 mean?"

"It means A, man. Concert pitch. Why."

"The tuner says 440 on the low A and 880 on the high one. Same note, one octave up. Double."

"Show me tomorrow."

Deej came over Thursday after cross-country practice, still in his spikes, and stood in James's room with the door shut because James's father had made it clear that the household had opinions about the trumpet after ten p.m. Deej played low A, watched the screen, played high A, watched it double, and said, "One octave higher vibrates at exactly twice the frequency. So that A above A440 is 880 hertz. That's what the screen's telling you."

"So it's not broken."

"It's the opposite of broken." Deej tapped the tuner with one muddy finger. "It's math."

James stared at the two numbers, 440 and 880, the way you stare at something that has been true your whole life without your permission. Everything he'd practiced on the clarinet, every scale, every etude, had been sitting on top of this the whole time, numbers underneath the notes like bones under skin. He didn't feel smarter. He felt late.

Friday night his father knocked once and came in without waiting. James lowered the horn. On the desk between them, the tuner's screen still glowed with the last note, an A held too sharp, the needle leaning right like a compass near a magnet.

"You sound better," his father said. Not kindly, not unkindly. Factually.

"It's math," James said. "The whole thing. I thought it was, I don't know, magic."

His father picked up the tuner, turned it over in his hands, and set it back down. "Your grandfather used to say you could tune a whole band off one note. I thought he was showing off." He stood there a moment longer, then said, "What time's this audition?"

"Ten in the morning. I still can't play the high part. The C above the staff. It comes out like a scream."

"Play it," his father said, and sat down on the bed.

James raised the horn. The tuner's needle woke and swung left, searching, and he pressed his lips together and thought about the number the C might be hiding underneath it, whatever doubling and doubling had built it, and blew.

story:
Christian kept the sample ballot folded in his back pocket all through fourth period, and by the time he sat down in Mr. Reyes's government class, the paper had gone soft at the crease. The room still smelled like the floor wax the custodian had laid down over the weekend, and the radiator under the window ticked in its own private meter. On the whiteboard, in Mr. Reyes's looping hand, was written: Election Day. Polls close at 7:00. Nobody checks whether you went.

Dara leaned across the aisle before the bell finished. "Are you voting after school or before?" she asked. "Because I have practice at four, and my mom said she'd drive us at five, but only if we're back by six."
"After," Christian said. "I have to eat first. My grandmother's making dinner early because of it." He said this as though it explained something, and in his family it did. His grandmother had announced on Sunday that she intended to feed him properly before his first vote, the way you might feed a boxer.
"You know," said Marcus from the row behind, "my brother didn't vote until he was twenty-three. Said it didn't matter." Marcus was seventeen and jaundiced about nearly everything, in the general way of seventeen-year-olds who have recently discovered that adults improvise.
"It matters to my grandmother," Christian said. At Sunday dinner she had told the story, unprompted, fork suspended over the potatoes. She had turned eighteen in 1970, she said, married already, working at the phone company, and she had not been allowed to vote. Not at eighteen. The law changing that, the amendment, was ratified in 1971, and it had taken about three months, faster than any other amendment to the Constitution. Christian had stopped chewing. Three months felt impossible. His mind kept trying to transmute the fact into something he recognized, some equivalent, and failing. He had said, "Wait, so people your age, they just, couldn't?" and his grandmother had laughed and said, "We could be drafted, honey. We just couldn't vote on anything," and his grandfather had put down his glass and left the table for a minute, which nobody commented on.

Mr. Reyes started class by asking who had registered, and eleven hands went up, which was more than Christian expected. "Good," Mr. Reyes said. "Now. Today's not a pep rally. I want you to look at the sample ballot and find one race you know nothing about. Raise your hand when you find it." Every hand went up again, slower this time. Christian's blank race was for a county water board, an office so obscure it sounded like something from a novel. "That's the honest part," Mr. Reyes said. "Not knowing. The dishonest part is pretending you know."
Christian copied the water board candidates' names onto a scrap of paper. He had been planning to skip that race entirely, to vote only where he had opinions, but something about the exercise annoyed him pleasantly, the way a pebble in a shoe makes you notice your own walking. Dara nudged him. "I'm asking my dad about the water one," she whispered. "He complains about our water pressure like it's a moral issue."

The class argued about whether a single vote mattered, and Marcus made his case with statistics he half-remembered, and a girl named Priya said that the argument itself was the point, that the vote was a kind of speech, and Christian found himself thinking about three months. About a whole country deciding, in a season, that eighteen-year-olds were citizens in the fullest sense. He had always assumed eighteen was simply when voting began, the way eighteen was when a lot of things began, a fact with no history, like gravity. It had a history. It had a grandmother at a table with a fork in the air.
"I read that the amendment setting the voting age at eighteen went through in about three months," he said, out loud, surprising himself. "In 1971. It was the fastest one ever ratified."
"Correct," Mr. Reyes said, and moved on to polling locations, because Mr. Reyes never gave speeches about anything, which was either modesty or strategy.

At five fifteen, Dara's mother's car smelled like hair spray and fast food, and the line at the elementary school gymnasium curved past the folding tables and out under a banner the PTA had made. Christian checked his watch too often. Dara's practice had been sacrificed; her coach had said "family thing?" and she had said "democracy thing," and that had been allowed. An older woman ahead of them in line dropped her pen and Christian picked it up, and she said, "First time?" in a way that suggested his face had already answered.
"How can you tell?"
"Everyone checks the machine like it's going to disagree with them." She smiled. "My husband was twenty when that amendment passed. He voted that same year. Talked about it until he died."

When Christian's turn came, the machine took his selections with small clicking sounds, each one a little louder in his ears than it could possibly have been. He voted for the things he knew. He came to the water board, the two unfamiliar names on his scrap of paper, and held his finger over them both. Dara was two machines away, frowning at her ballot with the concentration of someone defusing something. The clock above the gym door said 6:41.

He looked at the names a moment longer. Then he made his choice, and the machine clicked, and he stood there in the November light of the gymnasium wondering whether his grandmother, at her table right now with the good plates out, had ever once, in fifty years of voting, felt certain she was right.

story:
The bus smelled of diesel and grape juice, and Gabrielle had claimed the back seat with her knees up and the paperback open flat against them, running a pencil down the margin of chapter one. She had started the novel at seven that morning, finished it at lunch, and felt personally betrayed by page two hundred and something, and now she was going back to find every place the lying had started.

"You're rereading it already?" Dana dropped into the seat across the aisle, ponytail swinging. "It's been out since before my mom was born. It's called The Murder of Roger Ackroyd. Agatha Christie, 1926. You thought the butler did it?"

"Don't say anything else," Gabrielle said, holding up the pencil like a tiny fencing foil. "You already ruined my life once today."

"I told you the narrator did it. That's not ruining, that's education." Dana leaned over and tapped the cover, where a dignified doctor's face loomed. "Dr Sheppard. He narrates the whole book, and he's the murderer. The whole time. That's the trick."

Gabrielle had not believed her at first, because Dana's track record on spoilers included a French film she had described entirely wrong and an incident with a cake recipe. But the book club met Thursday, and the book club had chosen this novel specifically because Mrs. Okafor's list called it "the great experiment in unreliable narration," and Gabrielle wanted to walk in with evidence instead of outrage. So she reread, and the rereading was strange. Every sentence had two faces now. When Dr Sheppard wrote that he had a few things to dispose of, she had read it as a man tidying his papers; now it sat on the page like a wink she had missed. She flagged it. She flagged the paragraph where he described leaving the study and locked the gate behind him, unhurried, precise, a man with all the time in the world because he had made the time himself.

The bus jolted over the crossing on Miller Road and her pencil skidded a grey comet across the page. Behind her, Theo was narrating his own unreliable account of the basketball game to a row of freshmen, embellishing with every retelling. "And then I dunked it," he was saying, though Gabrielle had watched him miss twice.

"You fell," she called back over the seat. "I was there. You fell on Marcus."

"The narrator has a perspective," Theo said with dignity, and the freshmen laughed, and Gabrielle laughed too, because it was a joke, and also because it was exactly her homework.

By the time the bus turned onto the hill road she had nine flags, and she had begun to notice something odd, which was that Dr Sheppard never actually lied. He said he would not write certain things down. He said the reader would learn everything in due course. He was slippery the way a kid is slippery when you ask who broke the lamp, technically accurate, carefully incomplete. It reminded her of her own college application essay, three drafts of which had been truthful and none of which had been honest, and she had eventually shown the real one to her mother, which had gone better than expected, a small rapprochement achieved over the kitchen table and a plate of shortbread.

Dana migrated back a row and read over her shoulder, chin hooked on the seat. "Ooh, you found the gate bit. That's the famous one. Mr Kavliek talks about it every year, very incisive, he does a whole bit with a transparency."

"I want to find it myself first," Gabrielle said. "Before anyone explains it to me. Because the thing I keep wondering is whether I could have caught him, or whether the book doesn't let you. Whether it's a fair puzzle or just a trick."

"Maybe both," Dana said. "Maybe that's the point, that you trusted him for two hundred pages for no reason except that he was talking."

"Trust doesn't atrophy that fast," Gabrielle said, and then considered it. "Actually, maybe it does. One betrayal and I'm out here flagging commas."

The bus lurched to its stop and the aisle filled with backpacks and shoving. Gabrielle closed the book with the pencil still inside it, like a bookmark holding a case file shut. Thursday was two days away. She had the gate, the disposal line, the too-calm walk home, and a suspicion, still unproven, about the typewriter. She could be wrong about the typewriter. She had been wrong before, spectacularly, about the butler.

"Coming?" Dana said from the steps.

"In a second." Gabrielle stood in the emptying bus, thumb on the pencil, looking at the cover, where the doctor's face still looked trustworthy, in the way that faces do. She opened the book again to page nine and started walking down the aisle, reading, one hand trailing along the seat backs.

story:
Riley found the recipe at eleven in the morning, folded into the back of his mother's cookbook like a letter someone had started and never mailed. Chicken with lemon and herbs, for four. His parents were due home at six from the hospital where his grandmother had been since Tuesday, and his brother Marcus had texted from college that he was driving up, which meant dinner had to be real, not pasta from a box. Riley wanted to make the kitchen into a place people wanted to enter tonight, and he wanted to do it himself, without calling his mother to ask her anything.

He read the recipe through once, then again. Chopped parsley, lemon zest, garlic minced fine, a whole cut-up chicken, olive oil, butter, an egg for brushing the crust of the bread he'd decided to add because bread felt like an event. He liked the logic of a recipe, the way each sentence assumed the next one. He set the chicken in the sink to thaw the rest of the way and started chopping, and the kitchen began to smell like parsley and raw garlic, which was the smell, he thought, of something about to become dinner rather than the smell of dinner itself.

His phone buzzed on the counter. Marcus: "Is gran ok?" Riley typed "stable" and then deleted it and typed "we'll know more by tonight" and set the phone face down. He crushed the garlic instead, with the flat of the knife, because he'd seen a video once and wanted to know if it worked. It did. The clove split open under the blade like something unclasping, and he stood there a second, wondering how many things worked like that, how many things only needed to be pressed in the right place.

He browned the chicken in butter. That part went well, better than he'd expected, the skin going the color of an old photograph, and he moved the pieces to a plate and built the sauce in the same pan, scraping up the browned bits with broth while the juice of a whole lemon went in. Then he turned to the bread, softened the yeast in warm water, stirred in flour and salt, and reached into the refrigerator for the egg to brush on top before baking.

There were no eggs. Not one. The carton sat on the shelf with its lid open and nothing inside, and Riley stood holding it like a man reviewing his own solvency and finding the accounts empty. Marcus had made omelets on Sunday, apparently, all of them, and had said nothing, and Riley privately excoriated him for it, then felt the criticism dissolve, because would he himself have mentioned it? He would not have. He checked the bowl of dough rising under a towel on the counter, then the clock, then the recipe, where the egg was listed in the second line, in the ingredients, where he had not read carefully because he'd been reading for feeling the first time and for method the second.

The store was a fifteen-minute round trip if he ran. He could go, or he could skip the wash and bake the loaf plain, or he could start over on the bread entirely, and none of those felt like nothing. While he stood deciding, he thought about the cooking videos again, how the cooks always had every ingredient in little glass bowls before they started, chopped and measured and lined up, and he'd assumed that was for the camera, for show. Now he wondered if it was the whole point. If he had set out the egg this morning, an empty carton would have told him something at ten o'clock instead of at noon. He looked up the phrase on his phone with butter still on his thumb. Mise en place. It meant putting in place, measuring and preparing all the ingredients before starting to cook.

He ran to the store. On the way back, cutting through the park, he passed the small stone outcrop where his father had once shown him a sign about montane habitat, the kind of high, cold ground certain plants and birds needed, and Riley had asked whether the park could really count as montane and his father had said that depended on who drew the lines. He thought about that now with the eggs cold against his palm. His grandmother's doctors kept drawing lines too, saying she was stable and she was responding and she was not out of anything, and each word seemed to mean both more and less than it said.

He brushed the loaf with egg, sprinkled it with salt, and slid it into the oven. Then, because there was time, he took out every remaining ingredient for the rest of the meal and put them in bowls on the counter in a row: the chicken on its plate, the sauce waiting in the pan, the lemons, the parsley already chopped, the butter, the salt. It looked almost ridiculous, a dinner laid out like a still life, and he liked it anyway. Maybe the French cooks had it right and maybe it was just a way of pretending you could know the future, and Riley stood there unable to decide which it was, and not sure the two were even different.

The headlights came up the driveway at six-twenty, both cars, and Marcus's behind them. Riley took the bread out, set it on the rack to stop cooking, and heard the front door and his mother's voice saying something low to his father that he couldn't make out, which meant either very good news or very bad, and he would know in a moment and there was no bowl for that, no way to measure it out in advance. Marcus came into the kitchen first, dropped his bag, and stared at the row of little bowls on the counter.

"What is all this," Marcus said.

"Everything we need," Riley said, and wiped his hands on the towel, and went to find out about their grandmother.

story:
Elizabeth had claimed the corner table by the periodicals at three o'clock, and by five she had filled six pages of a legal pad with crossed-out sentences. Her paper was due in eleven days, and Mr. Okafor had rejected her first attempt with a single line of red pen: "This is a report. I asked for an argument."

The public library smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue. Outside, October was dismantling the maples along Bergen Street, and through the tall windows she could watch the leaves come down while she avoided the page. Her topic was the juvenile court system, whether sixteen-year-olds should be tried as adults for violent crimes, and she had chosen it because her cousin DeShaun had been tried as an adult at sixteen, in a courtroom Elizabeth had not been allowed to enter. She had been thirteen. Her mother had said, stay home, and she had stayed home, and she had never decided whether staying was loyalty or cowardice.

The problem was that she had facts but no position, or rather two positions, and each one wanted the whole page to itself. When she wrote from DeShaun's side, the sentences turned into a sermon, all heat and no hinges. When she wrote from the other side, the side her uncle the prosecutor would have taken, the prose went cold and evasive, hiding behind words like "accountability" without saying what they cost. She needed a way to hold both, and she did not know one.

At the next table, a boy from her AP US History class, Tomas, was slamming a style guide shut with theatrical despair. "Footnotes," he said to no one in particular. "Whoever invented these rules should be tried for crimes against students."

The reference librarian, a small woman named Ms. Prieto who wore her badge crooked, looked up from the returns cart. "The Chicago Manual of Style," she said. "Its notes-and-bibliography system uses footnotes. It was first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906."

Tomas stared. "Nineteen oh six?"

"That's older than my great-grandparents," he said, and seemed to find this genuinely troubling, as if the rules had acquired seniority, the right to be obeyed simply by outliving everyone who might have complained.

Elizabeth copied the call number from the spine when he set it down. She carried the Manual to her table and opened it, expecting bureaucracy, and found instead a kind of architecture. The footnotes were not decoration; they were a second argument running beneath the first, a quiet ledger of debts. Each note said: I learned this here, from this person, on this page, and you may go check. She thought of Mr. Okafor's red line, and of her uncle, and of DeShaun, and understood suddenly that an argument was not a fist. It was a claim standing on the record of what it owed.

She worked until the overhead lights clicked to their evening half. First she drafted a thesis she could actually defend: that transfer to adult court, whatever its logic for violent offenses, should require a judge's individual finding rather than automatic prosecution by statute, because DeShaun's case had turned on a mandatory statute and a judge who said, on the record, that his hands were tied. Then the footnotes, numbered, each one a small confession of source. When she reached for the case citation she found she could not remember whether the statute came from 2016 or 2018, and she wrote both possibilities on the pad and left a note to herself: check. The uncertainty did not feel like failure. It felt like honesty with a number attached.

She tried to explain this to Tomas on the way out, proselytizing a little, she admitted, the way anyone does after a conversion. "It's like the syntax of trust," she said. "Where the note goes, and what comes first, and what you admit you don't know. It's not sectarian, it's not one side's ritual. It belongs to whoever uses it honestly."

"You're describing paperwork," Tomas said, holding the door.

But walking home under the stripped maples, carrying the bag with eleven days of work in it, Elizabeth kept thinking about the ledger underneath, about 1906, about all the dead people who had argued in notes and been checked and been right or been corrected. And she thought again of the afternoon she stayed home, thirteen years old, obedient, sure that following a rule was the same as supporting a person. At the corner of Bergen and Sixth she stopped, took out her phone, and dialed the number for the county records office, the one she had found in the library's database but been afraid to use.

"Records division," a voice said. "We closed at five."

"Tomorrow, then," Elizabeth said, and put the phone away, and the manual, checked out in her name, sat in the bag on her hip, already three days overdue.

story:
Sophia's grandmother had always bought her tomatoes from the third stall on the left, the one with the crooked hand-painted sign, and so Sophia went there first, even though the tomatoes at the entrance looked just as good and were fifty cents cheaper a basket. The market had been going since seven and by ten the asphalt was giving back heat in slow waves. She held the list her mother had texted against the wind and worked down it: tomatoes, bread, a wedge of cheese, eggs from the Hsu farm if they still had any.

She was making dinner tonight, the whole thing, because her parents had driven to her aunt's to help move furniture and wouldn't be back until late, and because her brother Danny had asked her to, which he never did. He was leaving for basic training in three weeks and had requested one specific meal, their grandmother's pasta with fresh tomatoes and the slow-scrambled eggs she used to fold in at the end. Sophia had said yes before she understood what she was agreeing to, which was a kind of cooking that depended on a woman who had died in March.

The Hsus had eggs. She bought two dozen, more than she needed, because their carton was cold to the touch and it made her feel competent to plan ahead. Then she stood too long at a table of honey and jam, texting a friend about dorm assignments, and then longer still arguing pleasantly with the cheese man about whether pecorino or the cheaper local sheep's cheese was closer to what an Abruzzese grandmother would use. He gave her a taste of both. She bought the local one, then walked three stalls and turned around and bought a small piece of the pecorino too, because she could not decide, and because undecided felt, this summer, like its own small malaise she couldn't name.

It was past noon when she got home. She put the bags on the counter and stood in the kitchen with the door open behind her, letting the screen door bang the way her grandmother used to when her hands were full. The eggs sat in their bag. The cheese sat in its paper. The tomatoes, at least, she set out on the windowsill, because that was what her grandmother did, and the image of them there, fat and red against the glass, steadied her.

She cooked for two hours. The sauce took longer than the recipe card said, because the recipe card assumed you already knew things, assumed you knew that the garlic should barely color and that the tomatoes would give up their water if you just refused to hurry them. The eggs she scrambled on the lowest flame, stirring in figure eights, and when she folded them into the finished pasta the whole kitchen smelled like being eleven years old. Danny ate two plates and kept saying the word exactly, as in, this is exactly it, and their younger sister Lucy ate one plate and then asked if she could take the rest to her friend's house tomorrow because her friend's mother worked nights and never cooked.

So there were leftovers, a big steel bowl of them, and it was Lucy's question that made Sophia look at the clock. Four hours, she realized, since she'd left the market with the eggs, and the eggs had spent that time in a bag, then in the car, then on the counter while she cooked. She'd read something once, in the food safety unit of a class she'd half slept through, and now she dug through her phone to find it. Perishable food shouldn't sit between 40 and 140 degrees Fahrenheit for more than two hours. She read it twice. And one hour, the page said, if it's above 90 degrees out. She checked the weather app. Ninety-four.

"Where are the eggs?" she asked, and her voice came out sharper than she meant.

Danny, nonchalant, feet up on a chair, pointed at the counter. "Right there. Why?"

Sophia stood very still, holding the phone, doing the arithmetic. The eggs had been out at least four hours in a kitchen that had to be eighty-five, maybe more, with the oven running. The cooked pasta was newer, but it had been sitting out while they ate, and it was nowhere near the fridge. She thought of her grandmother, who left things out all day and waved off worry, and of her mother, who refrigerated butter. Two people she loved, two completely opposite instincts, and neither of them had ever stated a rule. She was tired of inheriting positions without reasons.

"The eggs are done," she said. "I can't use them. They've been in the danger zone way too long. The pasta I can save if I move it now, it's only been out about an hour, but the raw eggs are out." She heard herself and worried she sounded like a pamphlet, but Lucy was already looking at the bowl with narrowed eyes.

"So we can't give any to Kayla tomorrow?"

"We can give her the pasta. If it goes in the fridge right now." Sophia carried the bowl to the refrigerator, and the cold air on her wrists felt like arriving somewhere. She came back and scraped the eggs into the trash, all two dozen, the carton that had felt so reassuringly cold at eight in the morning. It was only money, she told herself, and then stopped telling herself things, because the loss was real and pretending otherwise was its own kind of dishonesty.

"You could've asked me," Danny said. "I know that stuff. We get it drilled into us. Two hours, one if it's hot out, above 90." He said it without any accusation, just handing her the fact the way you'd hand someone a tool they were already reaching for.

"You could've mentioned it four hours ago," she said, and he laughed, and she laughed, and then she went back to the recipe card and turned it over and wrote on the back, in her grandmother's old pencil stub, what she had learned, so that next time the knowledge would be in the family and not just in her phone. At the bottom she added the shopping order for a second attempt at the eggs, and under it a note to buy a cooler for the drive home from the market.

Then she texted her mother: pasta safe, eggs a loss, will contextualize later. And after a minute she picked up the pencil again and crossed that out and wrote, more simply, it's a long story, I'll tell you when you're home. She put the tomatoes back on the windowsill, the ones she hadn't cooked, and set one in the center of the sill where the light would find it in the morning.
