story:
The seminar room on the third floor of Hollis Hall had one window that faced the parking lot, which struck Jeremy as either poor planning or an accident of prophecy. Twelve students sat around a table with the professor, who had assigned them a city council transcript from a town called Fenwick, where the council had spent four hours arguing about whether to raise the downtown parking fee from two dollars to three. Jeremy had read it twice on the bus, twice more at his desk, and had underlined so many passages that the underlining had stopped meaning anything.

"Who wants to open," Dr. Okonkwo said, not quite making it a question.

Priya opened. She had prepared, which was her way of saying she had prepared. "The fee is too low," she said. "Three dollars still wouldn't cover the maintenance, and the overflow parking spills into the Elm Street neighborhood, so residents can't park in front of their own houses. The fee should be five."

Marcus countered that five dollars would push commuters to the mall on the highway, which would kill the downtown businesses, which would shrink the tax base, which would, he implied, eventually cause the heat death of Fenwick. A girl whose name Jeremy kept forgetting argued for a sliding scale by income. Someone else proposed validation stickers for local shops. The debate had the shape of an archipelago: eleven separate islands of argument, a thin channel of civility between each, no bridge anywhere.

Jeremy had not prepared a position. What he had was a memory, from the night before, of his roommate Dev scrolling past a meme and saying, "Oh, that's the Meadows thing," and refusing to elaborate because his show was starting. Jeremy had typed the name into the library database at midnight and found a 1997 essay about leverage points. He had read it in the common room under a diaphanous curtain of moths swarming the porch light, and certain sentences had rearranged the furniture in his head without asking.

He raised his hand, mostly to stop Priya from parametrizing the fee schedule any further. "Can I ask whether we're solving the right thing?"

"That's not a real objection," Priya said. "Everything is the right thing if you care about it."

"Sure. But the council spent four hours on the fee. Nobody asked why the city is organized so everyone drives downtown alone and leaves at five." He was aware his voice had gone up, and lowered it. "There's this essay. Donella Meadows, 1997, on leverage points. She argued that adjusting numbers like taxes or subsidies rarely changes a system much. Changing a system's goals, or the paradigm underneath it, changes the most."

Dr. Okonkwo's eyebrows did something small and interested, which Jeremy chose to read as encouragement.

"So the fee is a number," he went on. "We could fight about two dollars or three or five forever, and Meadows would say we're turning a dial that barely moves anything. If Fenwick actually wanted fewer cars downtown, the goal would have to change. Or the paradigm. The whole picture of what the street is for."

Marcus leaned back. "That's convenient. Your essay says the thing you want to argue can't be costed out."

"It's not my essay."

"It's also unfalsifiable," the girl whose name was, Jeremy now remembered, Talia, said pleasantly. "You can't run the experiment twice."

This was, Jeremy had to admit, true, and he said so, which in his experience of seminars was a tactical error, because admitting things invited more of them. Priya asked whether a paradigm was just a word people used when they didn't want to do math. Dr. Okonkwo asked whether Meadows herself had said anything about how paradigms get changed, and Jeremy had to say he'd gotten to the last section at two in the morning and remembered only the part about paradigms changing all the time anyway, in societies, without anyone planning it, which was either hopeful or terrifying depending on the century.

The problem, as Jeremy framed it for himself on the walk back across the quad, was that he believed two things at once. He believed Meadows, that the fee debate was a hall of small mirrors, and he believed Priya, that the residents of Elm Street needed relief this year and the fee was the lever actually attached to the machine. He had spent the seminar trying to get the two ideas to sit in the same chair, and they had refused, and he had ended by proposing, out loud, almost by accident, that Fenwick raise the fee to three and put the revenue toward a downtown where the fee itself could eventually shrink, which Marcus called incoherent and Talia called the only honest position anyone had taken all morning and Priya called a cop-out. He did not know which of them was right. He suspected that not knowing was, for the moment, the most accurate thing he had.

The parking lot below the seminar window had been nearly empty all morning, and Jeremy noticed, as they filed out, that it was nearly full. Somewhere a bell rang the hour. He stopped at the railing, took out his phone, and, instead of opening anything, just photographed the lot, rows of cars baking in the October sun.

"For the paradigm," Talia said, passing behind him.

He looked at the photo. "I was going to say for the fee."

"Same picture," she said, and walked on toward the science building, leaving him holding the rail and the phone and, for once, both of them.

story:
The rental truck followed them the whole way, and Morgan kept checking the side mirror to make sure it was still Dad behind the wheel and not some stranger hauling her boxes to a town she had agreed to only twice out loud. In the passenger seat, her grandmother sat with a road atlas open on her knees even though the phone was navigating, because she liked to know where she was in a way the phone never told her.

"You could have flown ahead with your mother," her grandmother said. "This is forty hours of road for a girl your age."

"I wanted to drive." Morgan had her own reason, though she had not said it in the car. Priya and Denae were meeting her at the pancake place on Route 9 at noon, one last breakfast before the truck got too far east to turn around. That was the plan. The plan had a hole in it, which was that after the pancakes there was nothing but four hundred more miles.

Grandma Ruth had her own want, and it had to do with the boxes in the truck. She was moving into the new house with them, giving up the apartment she had kept alone for nineteen years, and twice this morning she had asked whether the movers had wrapped her writing desk. She wanted, Morgan understood, to be the one who decided what got brought and what got left, and she was doing it by making lists on the back of a grocery receipt.

They stopped at the pancake place for fifty minutes. Priya was late and Denae was early and they split a short stack three ways, and Denae made a joke about Morgan's new town that started funny and turned vitriolic halfway through, about the people there, the kind of people who would love her, the kind who had never met her. Morgan laughed at the first half and then stopped laughing and said, "You don't know them either." Nobody said anything for a while after that. Priya took a photo of the three of them at the table, and it came out blurry, and she said she'd take another one, and then didn't.

The night before, they had all sat on Denae's garage roof, the way they had since seventh grade, and Priya had said the thing Morgan was now thinking about in the car. "It's not like we'll be strangers," Priya had said. "We'll text every day." And Denae had said, "No, we won't, we'll mean to," and it had sounded harsh but Morgan had known it was the more honest sentence. Friendship, she was beginning to see, was not only a feeling. It was a set of conditions, some of which nobody chose.

She had learned the actual evidence for that in June, killing time in the library while her mother packed dishes. She had been reading about college, about how to make friends in a place where nobody knew her, and she found a study from 1950 by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, and Kurt Back, done in student housing. The students had all been assigned their rooms more or less at random, which was what made it a study rather than an accident. The researchers found that people living closer together were more likely to become friends. People whose doors were near a shared stairway became friends more often too, because the stairway made them pass each other. Morgan read it twice. It wasn't shallow, she decided, or if it was, it was the shallow part of something real. You could love someone and never see them, and the love would sit there like a letter nobody opened.

"There's a stairwell apartment," Grandma Ruth said around dinnertime, somewhere in Ohio. "In the new house. Your father gave me the room by the back stairs."

"That's the Festinger room," Morgan said.

Grandma Ruth looked over. "The what?"

"Nothing. A study. People near the stairs make more friends. From 1950. Festinger, Schachter, and somebody named Back." She paused. "You'll be the popular one."

"I was planning on it," her grandmother said, and made a note on the grocery receipt.

Morgan texted Priya from a gas station outside Zanesville: ask Denae if she's still mad. Priya wrote back that Denae wasn't mad, she was just Denae, and then sent the blurry photo after all. Morgan looked at it under the fluorescent awning, three faces smeared by motion, and set it as her lock screen anyway. She did not know yet whether the study meant she should stop grieving the old friends or start forgiving the new ones in advance, or whether it meant nothing a person could act on at all. Probably, she thought, she would find out in September, and probably by accident, the way the students in the housing had. The truck's headlights swung into the lot behind them, and her father got out stretching his arms, holding the keys up so she could see them glint under the lights.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
Colton arrived at fifth period with the essay prompt already folded into his back pocket, though he had written nothing but a single underlined sentence: Who do you trust in Wuthering Heights, and why? He had read the whole novel in nine days, mostly on the bus, and somewhere around chapter nine he had begun to feel that the story kept catching in a filter, the way pond water looks different through a dirty jar.

Ms. Reyes had pushed the desks into a circle, which Colton hated, because circles demanded speech. She asked who narrated the book, and Drew Oliphant said Catherine, which was wrong, and then Priya said Heathcliff, which was also wrong, and then the room went quiet in the way rooms do when everyone is waiting for someone else to be wrong in a more interesting fashion.

"It's the housekeeper," Colton said, surprising himself. "Nelly Dean. Most of the book is her telling the story to this visitor, Lockwood. He's renting a house from Heathcliff, he gets sick, and while he's stuck there she tells him everything. So it's not like a normal narrator. Everything gets to us through both of them."

Priya leaned forward. "But wait. Didn't Nelly hate some of those people? Does that change how she tells it?" She had a pencil behind her ear and a paperback bristling with pink tabs. "Like, when she describes Catherine, is she describing Catherine or describing her own grudge?"

Colton opened his book to a page he had dog-eared without admitting it to himself. He had marked the spot where Nelly admits she warned Heathcliff about Hindley's plan to separate him from Catherine, an intervention that had consequences Nelly then narrated as though she had merely been a bystander. "She says she was only giving information," he said slowly, "but she chose which information. She's in the story and telling the story at the same time."

"That's an unreliable narrator," Priya said.

The phrase landed in Colton strangely, because he recognized the shape of it from somewhere outside the classroom. Last spring he had sat in his grandfather's kitchen while the old man explained, overCards and coffee, why Colton's mother didn't speak to her brother, and Colton had listened and believed every word, and only later, at Thanksgiving, heard his uncle's version of the same year, which matched his grandfather's in dates and almost nothing else. Neither man had lied, he thought now. Each had simply been the housekeeper of his own account, arranging the furniture of the past so that he stood in the most defensible corner of the room.

He said none of this aloud, but the inchoate idea pressed at him for the rest of the discussion. Drew argued that Lockwood was the bigger problem, a vain city man misreading everyone he met, and Colton found he could not entirely disagree, which unsettled him more than disagreement would have. If both narrators distorted, then the reader was left triangulating, and what he wanted, what the essay demanded, was a verdict. Trust or don't trust. He had assumed analysis meant sharpening a question until it cut one way.

After the bell he stayed behind, pretending to organize a binder that needed no organizing. Ms. Reyes asked if he had a question. He said not exactly, then asked it anyway: whether an essay could argue that you trust Nelly about some things and not others, that she might be accurate about weather and dishonest about motives, and whether that counted as an answer or just a refusal to choose.

She smiled and said the prompt asked who he trusted, not how much.

On the bus home he opened his notebook under the fogged window and wrote the word "scale" at the top of the page. Trust, he was beginning to think, was not a door you opened or kept shut; it was something with sentience of its own, an attention you paid in increments, adjusting as the evidence adjusted. He could not say that in an essay, or not in those words. But he could take the scene where Nelly watches Catherine through a keyhole and Heathcliff watches through the same keyhole, hearing two people he loves say two incompatible things about him, and he could ask what Nelly chose to keep, and what Lockwood chose to laugh at, and where the reader's own keyhole had been all along. He underlined a line of dialogue in the chapter, closed the book, and watched the houses slide past, each one holding, he supposed, somebody's version of the truth.

He got off two stops early and texted his mother: ask Uncle Ray about Thanksgiving 2016. Then he stood at the crosswalk, thumb still over the send button, and waited for the light.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
story:
The open house on Marsden Street was Blake's idea before it was his mother's, which surprised them both. He had seen the listing at eleven the night before, a flat above a shuttered bakery with a letting agent's name he didn't recognise, and by morning he had talked her into driving over, mostly because he wanted to see what £725 a month actually looked like when it stood in front of you as a room. The agent, a man named Dev with a lanyard and a folding table, was halfway through telling a young woman about the deposit when Blake and his mother came up the stairs.

"Two months up front," Dev was saying. "That's the deposit, plus your first month's rent in advance. Standard practice."

The woman, who introduced herself to nobody in particular as Priya, had a folder of printouts under her arm. She was maybe twenty-two, twenty-three, with the particular tiredness of someone who had viewed six flats this week. "Two months," she repeated, in a voice that suggested she had heard this number before and disliked it more each time.

"That's right." Dev had begun to pontificate about landlords needing security, about people who damaged properties, about the market being what it was, and Blake could see Priya's attention sliding off him the way his own did when a teacher covered material he already knew was beside the point.

She opened her folder. "The flat's £900 a month," she said. "That's under fifty thousand a year. So the deposit can't be two months. It's capped at five weeks' rent. I checked last night, the Tenant Fees Act 2019." She said it plainly, not triumphantly, the way you'd read out a bus timetable.

Dev's mouth opened and then reconsidered. Behind him, another couple had paused at the folding table, listening. "Five weeks," he said slowly, as if weighing a stone in his hand. "Right. Let me just call the office."

Blake drifted toward the kitchen while Dev stepped onto the landing with his phone. His mother followed, running her finger along the windowsill the way she did in every property they entered, an audit she performed without thinking. Blake had been doing the arithmetic since the listing: £725 a month, a deposit of five weeks, which meant five sevenths of a month's rent, which meant roughly £518. He did it again on his phone to be sure. And then the other number, the one that had brought him here in the first place: his mother's mention, three weeks ago and half a glass of wine into the evening, that she'd never owned, that she'd been paying other people's mortgages for twenty years.

"Mum," he said quietly, "if we put our rent money toward a deposit instead, what would that even take?"

She didn't stop looking at the windowsill. "A down payment, you mean. Different thing from a deposit, though everyone mixes them up. You pay a deposit to borrow a flat. A down payment buys you a stake in one." She turned around. "Ten percent, usually, for a first-time buyer with a mortgage. On a small place around here, that's fifteen, eighteen thousand."

Blake let the number sit. He had £2,400 saved from two summers of shelf-stacking, which had previously felt like a lot of money and now felt like a paragraph of a much longer book. "So the landlord's been collecting our rent for years," he said, "and that's been paying off his mortgage, and at the end we have nothing."

"That's the arrangement," his mother said. "It's not a betrayal. It's just what rent is." But she said it while looking at the little garden through the kitchen window, a strip of concrete with a stubborn rosemary bush in a pot, and Blake understood that explaining a thing and accepting it were not the same act.

On the landing, Dev came back in with the flattened posture of a man overruled by his own office. "Five weeks it is," he said to Priya. "I'll amend the paperwork. In advance, that's the first month's rent still, but the deposit comes down." Priya nodded and wrote the numbers in her folder, and Blake watched her do it, this small correction of a system by one person with a printout, and felt something adjust in his chest that he couldn't yet name.

He thought about his grandfather, who lived with a kind of grandiose asceticism, refusing heating in winter and calling it character while filling the house with enormous ornate furniture nobody could sit on. Saving money and wasting it, all at once, in the name of a story he told himself. Blake suspected the housing market had a bit of that in it too, people spending enormous sums to feel a certain way about themselves, landlords and tenants both.

Outside, Priya was on the steps, and Blake caught up with her before he'd decided to. "That thing you said, about five weeks," he said. "Would you send me where you found it? I'm trying to work all this out and I don't know anyone who's done it."

She looked at him, sixteen and earnest in his school coat, and something in her expression softened. "I'll send the link," she said. "Half the battle is knowing the rules exist. The other half I haven't worked out yet." She pulled her folder tight under her arm and started down the street toward the bus stop, and Blake stood on the steps with his mother's car keys in his hand, adding five weeks and ten percent and £2,400 together in his head, and then took out his phone and made a note of the number he got.

activity: graduating from high school
story:
Hayden had been carrying the folded printout in his blazer pocket for three days, and by graduation morning the paper had gone soft at the creases, the way money does.

The hallway outside the gym smelled of floor wax and carnations. He stood at his locker for the last time, turning the dial out of habit even though the locker was already empty, and Dana from his econ class stopped beside him with her cap mashed flat under one arm.

"You're still on about the wages thing," she said. It wasn't a question. Dana had spent the year building a spreadsheet of every scholarship in the state, and she wanted his essay in the class anthology because it had made their teacher, Mr. Ruiz, actually sit down.

"My uncle said it at dinner Friday," Hayden said. "He works at the community college. He told me workers twenty-five and older with a high school diploma earned eight ninety-nine a week, median, in 2023, and people without one earned seven oh eight." He recited it the way he'd recited it to himself in the shower, in the car, in the dark before sleep. "He said, that's your present, kid. That's what the paper's worth."

"That's not what the paper's worth," Dana said, but she didn't say what it was worth, and he noticed that.

The problem was that Hayden had written his exit essay, the one Mr. Ruiz had read aloud in April, about how a diploma measured nothing, how the whole ceremony was theater, a kind of polite nihilism dressed in robes. He'd been proud of the anger in it. Now the anger had a number attached, a small one, a hundred and ninety-one dollars a week, and the number refused to be romantic. He tried to transcribe the essay's argument into his notebook on the bench by the trophy case, to see whether it survived contact with what his uncle had said, and found that his own sentences looked petulant to him, a boy throwing his cap at the floor because the floor existed.

"Ruiz wants to read your name wrong," Dana said, watching him write. "He told me. He's been practicing."

"He won't read it wrong. It's two syllables."

"He reads everything wrong. He called me Dana with a hard E for a month." She fixed her cap on her head, crooked on purpose, because Dana wanted the yearbook photographer to catch it, wanted one image from the day that hadn't been arranged by adults. "My mother wants the cap straight. My whole family's coming straight-ward today. I'm the crooked element."

He laughed, and then the doors opened and the gym swallowed them, and the ceremony went the way ceremonies go, long and warm and strange. Mr. Ruiz did read his name wrong, "Hay-den" like two separate words, and Hayden walked the length of the gym with his hand out for a diploma case that turned out to be empty, a holder, the real one to be mailed in July after the office confirmed his detention hours had been served. He held it up anyway. His mother stood up in the third row and took a picture, and later he found the picture showed the case's emptiness clearly, the little window with nothing behind it, and he understood that his uncle's numbers and his own essay had both been about this case, one saying it was worth eight ninety-nine a week and the other saying it was worth nothing, and both of them talking about a piece of cardboard that hadn't even arrived.

Afterward, in the hallway, the one from that morning, now scattered with programs and a dropped carnation, his uncle found him. Uncle Marcel had the community college lanyard still on, though it was Saturday.

"So," Marcel said. "You got the eight ninety-nine version or the seven oh eight version?"

"Neither yet," Hayden said. "They mail it."

Marcel grinned, then didn't. "You know I wasn't trying to put a price on it. I was trying to say it matters. There's a difference."

"I know," Hayden said, and found that he did, mostly. What he couldn't say, what stayed uncertain even as he reached for it, was whether the diploma mattered because of the money or the money because of the diploma, or whether both of those were smaller than something his essay had been circling without landing on. He had spent a year learning to argue one side of things. Nobody had taught him how to hold two true sentences at once.

Dana appeared with her cap still crooked, holding her phone at arm's length. "The photographer got it," she said. "Look. My grandmother is frowning at me in the background and my mom is mid-yell. It's perfect. It's the only real picture anyone took today." She turned the screen toward Hayden and his uncle together, two witnesses, as if the picture needed certifying.

Hayden looked at it, the crooked cap, the frowning grandmother, the half-open gym doors behind them all, and thought that this was what he'd write next, if he wrote anything. Not that nothing mattered. Not that anything could be priced.

"So what's it going to be, kid," Marcel said, clapping him on the shoulder. "College or the seven oh eight?"

"College," Hayden said, and then, because the hallway was almost empty and the honest thing was easier out loud, "I don't know what for."

Marcel pulled the lanyard over his head and dropped it in Hayden's blazer pocket, right on top of the soft folded number. "Hold onto that too," he said. "It's worth exactly nothing a week."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
story:
Noah's first paycheque sat folded in his back pocket through the whole dinner shift, and between clearing plates he kept touching it the way you touch a sore tooth. He had worked thirty-one hours at Palmer's Grill over three weeks, and he had done the math in his head a dozen times: minimum wage times thirty-one, close to four hundred dollars. The cheque was for three hundred and eight.

The kitchen smelled of burnt butter and dish steam. He stacked plates too fast, chipped one, and slid it to the back of the rack where nobody would see. His plan had been simple. He needed two hundred and eighty for the used amp that Marcus was selling before he moved to Edmonton, and Marcus had said Friday, no later, because he needed the money for the move. Friday was tomorrow. Noah had counted on the cheque covering it with room to spare.

Under the fluorescents in the staff room, during his break, he unfolded the stub and read it slowly. Gross pay, four hundred and nine. Then lines he hadn't expected: CPP, EI, income tax. Each one small, but together they had eaten over a hundred dollars, and the income tax line was the strangest of all, because it said he would probably get most of it back in the spring, on something called a return. Money taken, then possibly returned. He understood that it was legal, since everyone at school who had jobs complained about it, but legal and fair were not the same word, and he wasn't sure yet which one this was.

What he did next felt less like curiosity than like gathering evidence. In the staff room there was a corkboard of old receipts the accountant had pinned up, and Noah pulled one from a supplier order and compared it to the customer bills in his apron. On the supplier receipt there was a separate line, GST five percent, added at the bottom. On the food bills there was nothing like it, because the tax was already inside the menu prices, or at least that was what he gathered from the way the totals worked out. He was still turning this over when the door chimed and a family came in, the father speaking with a flat, rounded accent that made Noah think of late-night television.

He took their order, brought the bread basket, and when he set down the bill the father squinted at it and then at his phone, where he had pulled up a photograph of a restaurant receipt from home. "Yours hides it," the man said to his wife, not quietly. "Back home there's VAT, twenty percent, and it's been that since the fourth of January, 2011." He tapped the photo. "Built into the price, but it's on the receipt, spelled out." Noah, clearing the next table, heard every word.

Later, at home, he looked it up on his laptop to be sure, because one overheard sentence wasn't evidence. It checked out, and he fell down a small rabbit hole of British receipts and Canadian ones, side by side, until his eyes ached. It seemed to him that there were two honest ways to do it: show the tax, or build it in. Marcus, over text, expatiated on the topic for six long messages, arguing that hidden taxes were endemic to governments everywhere, that they took your money in the dark so you'd stop noticing. Noah typed and deleted three replies. It wasn't exactly the dark. The number was right there on the stub, itemized, and on the UK receipt, itemized, and on the supplier's bill, itemized. Whether it felt like theft or like the price of roads and hospitals seemed, tonight, like a question of semantics dressed up as a principle. He wasn't ready to pick a side of that argument, and he noticed he didn't trust anyone who already had.

The withheld thing, the thing he hadn't told Marcus, was that the cheque was already spent in his mind. In the morning he would have to decide whether to ask his mother for a loan, which meant explaining the deductions, which meant admitting he'd expected four hundred and hadn't read anything about payroll before taking the job. He rehearsed it at the kitchen table while she stirred soup. "They take income tax off every cheque," he said, "but most of mine comes back on a return, because I won't earn enough this year to owe it. The other stuff, CPP and EI, that's gone for now." She nodded slowly, watching him. "So the number they advertise as your wage isn't your wage," she said. "Right," Noah said, and then, more carefully, "but it's not a lie either."

She lent him eighty dollars, and he made the handoff to Marcus in the school parking lot at lunch, the amp heavy and cold through his jacket. Marcus counted the bills, and Noah watched him count, and thought about how much of every dollar in Marcus's palm had already been taxed before it reached his hand, and how much would be taxed again when Marcus spent it, and how little of that either of them would ever see written down. "You okay?" Marcus asked. Noah hefted the amp into his locker. "Yeah," he said. "Carry it for me. It's heavier than it looks."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
story:
Sebastian had agreed to spend the last week of August at his grandparents' house on the condition that he could use the darkroom in the basement, which his grandfather had built in 1974 and never dismantled. The application to art school was due in November, and the requirement that frightened him most was not the ten artworks but the statement, the single page in which he was supposed to explain what held them together. He had chosen self-portraits as his theme, mostly because he had a camera and no other subject, and already the problem had revealed itself: on his third day, tacking contact sheets to the corkboard above the drying rack, he counted eight versions of the same narrow face squinting into the same lens.

"Your grandfather kept saying you'd find it down there," his grandmother called from the top of the stairs. She had her own project that week, a stack of his grandfather's framed prints she wanted to sort through and donate to the library, and she wanted Sebastian's opinion on which ones. He heard her slippers scuffing on the linoleum above him for hours at a time, the particular hush of someone preserving something.

Between trays of developer he wandered the shelves. His grandfather had been a genuine aesthete, a man who arranged even his WD-40 and his masking tape with a curator's care, and the art books were ordered by decade. Sebastian pulled down a heavy one with a black spine, opened it on the workbench beside the safelight, and stopped. Face after face, all the same woman, and none of them the same person: a secretary, a hitchhiker, a woman in a slip looking out a window as if the street below held a verdict. He checked the caption. Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, 1977 to 1980. Seventy black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.

He sat on the stool with the book open across his knees. Seventy, and every movie invented. She hadn't taken pictures of herself; she had taken pictures of a whole population that happened to share her face. Was that dishonest, or was it more honest than anything, since a person contains all those people anyway? He turned the pages slowly, wondering whether the woman in the slip had ever existed anywhere except in the moment the shutter opened, and deciding that maybe that was the only place anyone exists.

"Do you want soup or leftover chicken?" his grandmother called down that evening. He climbed the stairs with the book under his arm and found her at the kitchen table with the donation pile, three frames face down, two face up, a pencil tucked behind her ear like a carpenter. He noticed the pencil, the reading glasses pushed low, the small wet shine on one cheek she had not wiped.

"Grandpa had this," she said, tapping the cover. "He said it underpinned half of what people did with cameras afterward. I never liked them, honestly. All that pretending." She looked up. "Which of these should the library get? He'd have wanted you to choose."

He chose two for her, a foggy ferry dock and a portrait of her at thirty, and watched her hold that one a long moment before setting it aside from the donation pile, apart from the others, face up on the counter. She wanted him to take her to the library on Thursday to deliver them, and he said he would, and he did not say that Thursday was his deadline to mail the first draft of his statement.

In the darkroom the next morning he tried it. He put on his grandfather's gray cardigan and photographed himself at the window with a suitcase, then in his father's old work shirt with a toolbox, then simply as a boy looking at a darkroom door as if it led somewhere. The camera did not care who he was; it cared who he was pretending to be, and the pretending, he was starting to think, was not a mask over the truth but a way of auditing it. Still, the uncertainty stayed with him like the smell of fixer on his hands. Whether a portfolio of disguises added up to a self, or just to ten deflections from one, he could not yet say, and he wrote that sentence down and then crossed it out and then wrote it again.

Thursday morning he carried the framed ferry dock and the frame of his grandmother at thirty to the car while she locked the front door twice, the way she did. The artist's statement sat folded in his jacket pocket, one page, still provisional. In the passenger seat his grandmother rested the portrait of herself face down against her knees, then, as he backed out of the driveway, turned it over.

"Drive past the water before the library," she said. "Just once."

story:
The art shed at Camp Wanoka smelled of cedar shavings and bug spray, and Lily had claimed the corner table by the window on the first day, which she now considered the single best decision of her summer. She was working on a drawing of the lake for the end-of-session exhibition, a wide panorama with the dock in the foreground and the far shore dissolving into hills. Her counselor had offered the campers a choice between painting and drawing, and Lily had chosen drawing because she wanted the picture to feel precise, the way a photograph feels precise, every plank of the dock distinct.

For three days it had gone well. Then the rain came, the humidity thickened, and the drawing began to smudge. The dark water of the lake spread its shadow upward into the sky whenever her sleeve crossed the paper, until it looked as though the hills were dissolving in a fog that had no business being there. She rubbed at it with a kneaded eraser and made it worse, a gray haze blooming across what had been clean white space.

"Which grade did you use?" asked Marcus, dropping onto the stool across from her. He was the boy from Cabin Four who drew dragons with obsessive detail, and he had a tin of pencils arranged like surgical instruments. Lily turned her pencil over and read the letter stamped on the barrel. "Six B, it says."

"That's your nemesis right there." He held up his own pencil, a thin pale thing. "A pencil's core is graphite mixed with clay. More clay makes it harder and lighter, and those are the ones marked H. Less clay makes it softer and darker, and those are marked B." He rolled the tin toward her. "You've basically been drawing with charcoal wearing a disguise."

Lily sat with that for a moment. She had always assumed darkness was simply a matter of pressing harder, that effort itself made the mark. The idea that darkness was built into the tool, decided before her hand ever moved, bothered her in a way she could not immediately name. She picked up an H pencil and made a test stroke on the corner of a scrap. The line was so faint she had to tilt the paper toward the window to see it, pale as a hair, and when she dragged her thumb across it, nothing smudged at all.

She thought of her grandmother's kitchen table, where she had learned to draw at seven or eight, sprawled across the vinyl tablecloth with a single soft pencil from a junk drawer. Her grandmother had never taught her anything about materials; she had only slid biscuits across the table and said, "Draw the sugar bowl, sweetheart, draw it just as it is." Lily had pressed and pressed to get the shadow under the bowl dark enough, tearing the paper once, and her grandmother had laughed and said the shadow could be whatever color Lily wanted, because drawings weren't under oath. That had felt like freedom then. She had never thought to ask whether a different pencil existed.

Now she laid the two test strokes side by side on the scrap, the deep feathered smear of the 6B and the disciplined whisper of the H, and she understood that neither one was the true one. The hard pencil gave her the control she wanted for the dock planks and the far hills; the soft one gave her the weight of the water and the mass of the pines. She had been trying to codify her whole drawing into a single method, one way of making a mark, when the panorama needed both. She began the lake over again on fresh paper, blocking the sky and water with the 6B in loose sweeps, then trading it for an H to pick out the dock, its railing, the far shoreline, letting the hills stay half-suggested.

It was slow, and it was not clean. Sometimes she pressed the soft pencil too hard where the hard one belonged, and the bank of the lake blurred again, and she lifted the paper and blew across it and kept going. Marcus drifted back after dinner and watched without comment, an epicurean silence about him, savoring her struggle the way he savored the precise suffering of getting a dragon's wing membrane right. He did reach over once and rotate her paper so her sleeve would stop crossing the wet graphite, and she said thanks without looking up.

On the last night before the exhibition, the drawing was finished in the only sense that mattered to her, which was that she had stopped. The lake held its darkness without bleeding into the sky, and the hills were pale and far, and the dock stood crisp and quiet above the water. She tacked it to the exhibition board between a painted canoe and Marcus's dragon, stood back, and found that she still did not know whether the picture was good, or only finished, and that the two might not be the same thing, and that she could live with not knowing. Marcus came and stood beside her, arms crossed, studying the dock.

"Which one is that," he said, "the H or the B?"

Lily pointed at the hills, then at the water, and said, "Both."
